summary:
RedRoute is a survival guide for a walk on Mars. It uses two linked screens on the same route, both carried by the astronaut: a mission tablet to plan and review the outing, and a helmet visor that guides the walk hands-free. RedRoute is designed for any point on Mars: the more data it receives about an area, the more routes it can calculate there. For this prototype we used Mount Sharp, in Gale Crater, as a sample area, where the Curiosity rover has worked since 2012.

NASA tools show Mars at a regional scale. RedRoute zooms in to the area of a single outing and puts the astronaut's safety first. It plans routes over real 1 m terrain and HiRISE imagery, avoiding steep slopes, soft sand, sharp rocks and radio dead zones. At every point of the route, it checks that the astronaut can walk back to the habitat before running out of oxygen. It also tracks radio line-of-sight, shelter, radiation and cold. An onboard AI assistant answers questions using only the outing's data, while alerts and emergency protocols follow fixed rules.

This matters because future crews will need to make life-or-death decisions far from any help. RedRoute turns open NASA data into clear, on-the-spot answers to two questions: "Where can I go?" and "Can I make it back?"
details:
WHAT IT DOES

RedRoute is a survival guide for a walk on Mars, built at the scale of a single walk. Tools like Mars Trek and the USGS-NASA geologic maps show Mars by region; a walk fits in a few kilometers. At that scale, an astronaut in a suit needs direct answers: where to step, how far is left, whether the radio reaches the habitat, and whether the oxygen covers the walk back.

RedRoute is designed for any point on Mars: the more data it receives about an area, the more routes it can calculate there. For this prototype we used Gale Crater as a sample area, one of the best-studied places on Mars.

Two screens share the same route, and both go with the astronaut:

- Mission tablet: plan the outing before leaving the habitat and check or change the plan along the way. It opens on a 3D globe of Mars and zooms into a 3D map with real terrain and imagery. Each click on the map becomes a stop; the route visits every stop and comes back along the safest path, on foot or by vehicle. A time-of-day slider moves the Sun and shows how much daylight is left. A safety panel shows oxygen, radio, sand and shelter before anyone leaves.

- Helmet visor: keeps the view of the terrain clear, with only heading, next stop, O2, battery and time to walk back on screen. A guide line on the ground leads to the next stop. Alerts appear by severity, and emergency protocols are run step by step. Everything else opens on demand, by touch or by voice.

Sample outing, "From clays to sulfur": a traverse of Mount Sharp next to Curiosity's path that follows the history of water in Gale Crater, from ancient lake clays to pure sulfur stones and sulfate layers. On foot, starting at 10:00, calculated on real terrain: 9.0 km round trip, 6 h 44 min, +482 m of climb, 19.9° maximum slope and 3 science stops, each with a scientific question, a sampling task and its sources.

HOW IT WORKS

- Six NASA data types on the same ground: optical (HiRISE, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter), topographic (USGS 1 m elevation model), thermal (THEMIS, Mars Odyssey), atmospheric (REMS, Curiosity), radiation (RAD, Curiosity) and geologic (USGS-NASA geologic map). Live Curiosity data is read from public NASA services when the app opens.

- Routes: A* pathfinding over the terrain using Tobler's hiking function, avoiding steep slopes, soft sand, sharp rocks and areas without radio contact.

- Walk-back check: from any point, oxygen must cover the walk to the habitat at 2 km/h (NASA's planning speed) plus a one-hour reserve.

- Radio: a straight line of sight from the suit antenna to the habitat. In the sample traverse, 81% of the route has no direct line of sight, and the panel shows this before departure.

- Shelter, Sun and cold: the nearest terrain shelter is marked; the Sun position comes from NASA's Mars24 algorithm; cold warnings appear on the tablet and one hour ahead on the visor.

- Emergencies: dust storm, solar particle event, radio loss and vehicle failure each have a protocol, guided step by step on the visor.

- Onboard AI: a language model acts as the onboard computer. With every question it receives the outing data of that moment, can call tools (plan, stops, protocols, source search, calculator) and answers "what if" questions such as "What if I go by vehicle?". Every number in an answer is checked against the data before it appears. Alerts and emergency protocols follow fixed rules and never depend on the AI.

- Transparency: every Mars number is labeled on screen as Real, Calculated, Hypothesis or Simulated, and the full source list is in the tablet panel.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Safety first: the walk back is planned before the science.

- The right scale: NASA data brought down from regional maps to the few kilometers of a real outing.

- One plan, two screens: the tablet and the visor always show the same route.

- Trustworthy AI: grounded answers, and safety logic that does not depend on the AI.

We want to show that open NASA data, combined at the scale of a single walk, can help future crews make safer decisions on the surface of Mars. Next steps: detect smaller rocks with the 25 cm HiRISE imagery, validate the oxygen numbers against real spacesuit data, and add new areas of Mars as more data becomes available.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It starts from the walk back, not from the destination: every point of the route is checked against oxygen, radio and shelter.

- An AI that cannot invent numbers: every figure it says must come from the outing data.

- Honest data: every value on screen says whether it is real, calculated, a hypothesis or simulated.

- Planning and execution in one system: the same route on the tablet and on the helmet visor.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Astronaut safety: oxygen reserve, radio coverage, radiation, cold, shelter and emergencies.

- Mobility in a suit: slope limits, soft sand, sharp rocks and walking speed.

- Mars realities: there is no GPS on Mars, so the astronaut's position is simulated in the prototype.

- Data limits: the 8 m terrain grid hides small rocks, sand is estimated from image color, and the emergency protocols are the team's proposal.

TOOLS AND SOFTWARE

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step; Three.js for the 3D terrain, globe and visor.

- A* pathfinding, Tobler's hiking function and NASA's Mars24 sun-position algorithm.

- Onboard AI (prototype choice): openai/gpt-6-luna through OpenRouter on the published site; qwen3:14b through Ollama when run locally.

- Voice (prototype choice): Kokoro-82M for speech and Whisper for speech recognition.

- Hosting (prototype choice): Vercel serverless functions, plus a Docker image for self-hosting.

These AI, voice and hosting tools were chosen only to build and demonstrate the prototype. We are aware that a real mission would need different tools: for example, a language model and voice models running locally on the habitat and suit hardware, with no dependence on cloud services on Earth.

USE OF AI

We used Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding assistant. The idea and the features were designed by the team, which also reviewed and tested the code. The demo video and its voice-over were generated with AI and carry a visible watermark. No AI-generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
